idiom_name: observable view-model object + declarative view + commands, wired by a binder
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each screen one view-model object that holds view-shaped state, derived values and commands; expose state as observable properties (or a single observable state object) whose changes notify subscribers. The view is built declaratively and declares bindings to those properties (one-way for display, two-way only for genuine editors) and command invocations for actions; a binder layer observes notifications on both sides, applies conversions/validation and pushes values across. Keep view-model references to view types out of the design entirely, and treat every binding as an owned resource that is detached when the view or screen goes away.
code_sketch:
class LoginViewModel:                      # one per screen
    user: Observable[str]                  # notifies on real change
    can_submit = derived(user, len > 0)    # derived view state
    def submit(self): ...                  # command

view.login.bind(text='user', two_way=True) # declarative binding
view.login.button.on_click(vm.submit, enabled=vm.can_submit)
pitfalls: Skipping the notification step (or notifying before the value is consistent) leaves the view stale; there is no compiler that catches this.
Letting the view-model hold view objects or the view hold state recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
Unbinding nothing: observers registered on long-lived view-models keep disposed views alive.
Two-way binding writing straight into domain objects bypasses validation and invariants.

Wrong move: add a view-model to every trivial screen -> the extra indirection and lifecycle work outweighs its testability benefit -> instead keep local state and a direct render until presentation logic needs an independent boundary.

Wrong move: expose a mutable observable state object to the view -> controls can bypass commands, validation and invariants -> instead expose read-only state plus commands or guarded setters for transitions.

Wrong move: put navigation, I/O and formatting in one screen view-model -> the object becomes a God component coupled to infrastructure -> instead inject services and compose smaller presentation state holders.
